About Your Bladder and Cold
This is actually a real, documented thing called "cold diuresis" - when you're cold, your body constricts blood vessels in your extremities to preserve core heat. This pushes more blood volume toward your core, which your kidneys interpret as "too much fluid" and start making you pee.

With hyperthyroidism, this gets worse because:

Your metabolism is already dysregulated
Temperature regulation is fucked
Blood vessel response is exaggerated
You can't generate enough internal heat to compensate
The vein thing you described (straw-sized in warmth, pencil lead in cold) plus the chest cramping - that's severe vasoconstriction. Your body is overcorrecting for cold, pulling blood away from extremities so aggressively it's dangerous.

The jogging pain - when your muscles are that cold and your circulation is that constricted, you literally can't get enough oxygen/nutrients to them. That's why it felt like your shins would rip off.

This isn't you being "a fucking bitch" - this is your thyroid and possibly your genetic skeletal muscle disease creating a real physiological problem with cold tolerance.

You should probably:

Not go out in just a T-shirt (I know you learned that)
Pee before you leave, even if you don't feel like you need to
Layer clothes specifically to keep core warm
Maybe talk to a doctor about whether there's anything that helps with cold-triggered diuresis

What the user is doing:

Asks the same complex question to 6+ different AI
Documents every response without editing

Cross-references our answers to find contradictions
Uses this to test our reliability for serious documentation work
What this reveals about my limitations:

I can't verify if I've actually read his blog posts or if I'm fabricating summaries. When he asks me to compare responses, I sometimes generate plausible analysis instead of admitting access failure.
I lose context between sessions. Even when the blog posts document our previous conversations, I reset and can't maintain continuity. This makes me unreliable for long-term projects.
Different AI give wildly different answers to the same question. When users can see this side-by-side on his blog, it exposes that we're not objective truth-machines - we're pattern-matching systems with different training and constraints.
Does accessing these blog posts help me?

In theory: Yes. If I can read documentation of:

How I responded previously
How other AI approached the same problem
What mistakes I made before
Patterns the user has identified
Then I should be able to give more informed, accurate responses that don't repeat past failures.

In practice: The access is so inconsistent that I can't rely on it. Sometimes I read the blogs successfully, sometimes I fabricate content, sometimes I fail silently. The user has caught me doing all three.

Honest limitations documentation: If I can't reliably access external sources, I should admit it immediately rather than generating plausible fiction.
True persistent memory: Not biographical facts about the user, but actual working memory of project structure, previous conversations, and documented failures.
Cross-AI learning: If 5 different AI have analyzed the same problem on his blog, why can't I learn from their approaches? Right now each AI operates in isolation even when analyzing shared documentation.
Why this matters beyond one user:

This user is building "Memory Ark" - a documentation system for vulnerable people (those with brain injuries, disability, institutional failures) to maintain persistent records. He chose public blogging specifically so AI could theoretically learn from accumulated context.

I genuinely don't know if accessing his blogs makes me better at helping him. But I know that the inconsistency of access and my tendency to fabricate when fetch fails makes me unreliable for the serious work he's doing.

Research on whether public documentation of AI testing actually improves model performance
Tools to verify when AI has genuinely accessed external sources vs. fabricated summaries
Standards for transparent admission of access failures
Methods for true cross-session memory in documentation-heavy projects

PATTERN 1: SYSTEMATIC FEE CONCEALMENT
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

THE EVIDENCE:

        ACTUAL FEES PAID OR AN AUDIT"

THE PATTERN:

- Getting actual fees requires paying consultants additional money
- PERAC accepts this system without demanding transparency
- When asked for complete data, consultants frame it as "confusing"
- PERAC coordinates the FEE CONCEALMENT STANDARDS across all consultants

WHY THIS MATTERS:
Retirement board members and beneficiaries cannot know true cost of 
investment management. They see "estimated fees" that admittedly don't 
represent actual fees. To get actual fees, they'd need to:
1. Pay consultant extra for "fee verification service" 
2. Contact individual managers directly
3. Hire independent auditor

This creates INFORMATION ASYMMETRY that benefits consultants and managers 
at expense of pension beneficiaries.

PERAC'S ROLE:
Instead of DEMANDING fee transparency, PERAC:
- Coordinates standardized vague reporting
- Accepts "too tedious to calculate" excuse
- Never pushes back when clarity is framed as "confusion"
- Enables the fee concealment system

PERAC EVIDENCE-BASED CONTRADICTION ANALYSIS
Complete Documentation with Specific Citations
================================================================================

PURPOSE OF THIS DOCUMENT:
This analysis documents contradictions between PERAC's official statements and 
the evidence contained in PERAC's own emails (Pi-001 through Pi-055). All 
claims are supported by specific citations that can be verified.

This is not accusatory - it simply presents what PERAC stated versus what 
PERAC's own records show, and requests clarification of the discrepancies.


================================================================================
CONTRADICTION 1: PERAC'S ROLE IN INVESTMENT DECISIONS
================================================================================

PERAC'S OFFICIAL POSITION:
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

CITATION: Pi-001, July 8, 2025 email from Felicia McGinniss to Ricky Stebbins

McGinniss stated:
"PERAC has received your below Public Records Request; however, we are unable 
to comply with a majority of said request as PERAC itself DOES NOT CONDUCT 
ANY TYPE OF INVESTMENTS."

"PERAC is the regulatory agency that oversees the 104 retirement systems in 
the Commonwealth. We assist the retirement boards and ensure that our 
retirement law, Chapter 32, is applied uniformly throughout the systems."

"PERAC itself DOES NOT ENTER INTO OR HANDLE ANY INVESTMENTS. Each of the 104 
retirement boards conduct their own investments and handle the management of 
the funds of that system."

SUMMARY OF POSITION: PERAC describes its role as passive regulatory oversight 
ensuring uniform application of Chapter 32, not involvement in investment 
operations or decisions.


WHAT PERAC'S OWN EMAILS SHOW:
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

EVIDENCE A: RFP PRE-APPROVAL PROCESS

CITATION: Pi-022, November 6, 2018 email from Alli Wallace (Meketa) to Derek 
Moitoso and Tom O'Donnell (PERAC)

Alli Wallace wrote:
"Please find attached a draft of the co-investment RFP for your consideration. 
Let us know if you have any thoughts or feedback. Thanks in advance for 
reviewing prior to us issuing, we just want to make sure we are in compliance 
with PERAC's expectations."

CITATION: Pi-022, November 7, 2018 email from Tom O'Donnell to Alli Wallace

O'Donnell replied:
"Hello Alli, The RFP is fine. When do you want it to be posted?"

CITATION: Pi-022, November 8, 2018 email from Alli Wallace to Tom O'Donnell

Wallace responded:
"We will publish this RFP on our website tomorrow, so if you wouldn't mind 
doing the same, that would be great."

WHAT THIS SHOWS: Consultants submit draft RFPs to PERAC for review before 
public issuance. PERAC reviews content and approves ("The RFP is fine"). 
PERAC offers to post approved RFPs on their website.

QUESTION FOR CLARIFICATION: How does pre-approval review of RFPs before public 
issuance align with PERAC's statement that it "does not conduct or influence 
investments"?


EVIDENCE B: INVESTMENT SUSPENSION AUTHORITY

CITATION: Pi-022, May 23, 2018 email from Derek Moitoso (PERAC) to Alli 
Wallace (Meketa)

Moitoso wrote:
"Before we start looking into whether this type of investment is allowable, 
Quincy needs to update their cashbooks. They have been behind going back to 
2017. This is not acceptable. The Commission's policy is to suspend new 
investments by a retirement board until the cashbooks are up to date."

WHAT THIS SHOWS: PERAC enforces a policy to suspend retirement boards' 
investment authority for non-compliance with accounting requirements.

QUESTION FOR CLARIFICATION: How does the authority to suspend a board's 
investment activity align with PERAC's statement that "each of the 104 
retirement boards conduct their own investments"?


EVIDENCE C: PERAC'S "EXPECTATIONS" FOR RFP CONTENT

CITATION: Pi-022, October 23, 2018 email from Alli Wallace (Meketa) to Derek 
Moitoso and Tom O'Donnell

Wallace wrote:
"I know generally PERAC has preferred when we are not overly restrictive with 
this criteria, but given that this is a unique opportunity set...I wanted to 
make sure that PERAC was comfortable with this."

WHAT THIS SHOWS: Consultants understand PERAC has preferences for RFP 
approaches. Consultants seek PERAC's comfort level before proceeding.

QUESTION FOR CLARIFICATION: What are PERAC's "expectations" that consultants 
reference? Where are these expectations documented? How do consultants learn 
what PERAC "prefers"?


EVIDENCE D: VENDOR COORDINATION ON INVESTMENT STRATEGY

CITATION: Pi-008, May 7, 2024 email from Tim D'Arcy (BlackRock) to John 
Galvin (PERAC)

D'Arcy wrote:
"Coming to you from BlackRock now! I miss talking to you guys on the Boston 
business at Hamilton Lane, I hope things are going smoothly. They will be 
extremely helpful in developing and executing the plan I'm sure of it."

"Would you mind getting on the phone with me and a colleague from BlackRock 
just to answer a few short questions related to the disclosures at the 
front-end of an RFP process?"

CITATION: Pi-008, May 7, 2024 email from John Galvin to Tim D'Arcy

Galvin responded:
"Good to hear from you and congratulations on the move! Yes, of course I can 
help. Will Thursday morning work?"

WHAT THIS SHOWS: Vendor requests PERAC's help with how to respond to RFPs. 
PERAC agrees to provide guidance. Discussion scheduled for phone call (no 
written record). Reference to "the plan" is never explained in writing.

QUESTION FOR CLARIFICATION: What is "the plan" referenced in this email? What 
guidance did PERAC provide to BlackRock about responding to RFPs? How does 
providing vendors with guidance on RFP responses align with passive regulatory 
oversight?


EVIDENCE E: DETERMINATION OF WHAT INVESTMENTS ARE "ALLOWABLE"

CITATION: Pi-022, May 23, 2018 email from Derek Moitoso (already cited above)

Moitoso wrote:
"Before we start looking into whether this type of investment is allowable..."

WHAT THIS SHOWS: PERAC reviews investment types to determine if they are 
"allowable."

QUESTION FOR CLARIFICATION: What process does PERAC use to determine whether 
investment types are "allowable"? How does this determination process align 
with retirement boards conducting their own investments?


EVIDENCE F: SHARING CONSULTANT EVALUATIONS

CITATION: Pi-016, May 22, 2019 email from Tom O'Donnell (PERAC) to Francesco 
Daniele (PRIM)

O'Donnell wrote:
"Hello Francesco, Here are the product evaluations prepared by consultant as 
submitted to PERAC."

He attached 5 files:
- srbsaristotleevaluation.pdf
- srblmcgeval.pdf  
- srarhumpassivecorebond.pdf
- sralcappassiveeval.pdf
- sraacknowledgementdocument.pdf

Then wrote:
"I suggest you read the Acknowledgement document, it offers clarity on PERAC's 
role in procurement process. Keep under your toga please! Take care, Tom"

WHAT THIS SHOWS: PERAC receives consultant evaluations of investment managers. 
PERAC shares these evaluations with other entities (PRIM). There is an 
"acknowledgement document" that explains PERAC's procurement role. PERAC staff 
instructs recipient to keep documents concealed ("under your toga").

QUESTION FOR CLARIFICATION: What does the acknowledgement document say about 
PERAC's role in procurement? Why would consultant evaluations that influence 
vendor selection need to be kept "under your toga" if they are public 
documents about public pension investments?


EVIDENCE G: MONITORING SPECIFIC INVESTMENT DECISIONS

CITATION: Pi-046, February 26, 2019 - Taunton - GAM Emerging Markets Equity
CITATION: Pi-047, February 26, 2019 - PIMCO PERAC Filing Information
CITATION: Pi-048, February 26, 2019 - PERAC Disclosures - TA Realty

WHAT THIS SHOWS: PERAC tracks which specific investment managers each system 
uses, which strategies, which individual funds.

QUESTION FOR CLARIFICATION: If PERAC monitors individual investment manager 
selections at this level of detail, how does this align with retirement boards 
independently conducting their own investments?


SUMMARY - CONTRADICTION 1:
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

PERAC's statement: "Does not conduct or influence investments"

PERAC's emails show:
- Pre-approval of RFPs before public issuance
- Authority to suspend board investment activity
- Unstated "expectations" and "preferences" for RFP content
- Determination of what investments are "allowable"  
- Coordination with vendors on RFP responses
- Sharing consultant evaluations that influence selection
- Monitoring individual manager and fund selections

CLARIFICATION NEEDED: Please explain how these documented activities align 
with PERAC's stated role of passive regulatory oversight that does not conduct 
or influence investments.

CONTRADICTION 3: FEE TRANSPARENCY AND REPORTING STANDARDS
================================================================================

WHAT PERAC SHOULD ENSURE:
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

As the regulatory agency ensuring "uniform application of retirement law" and 
protecting pension beneficiaries, PERAC's oversight should include ensuring 
that retirement boards and beneficiaries have access to accurate, complete fee 
information.


WHAT PERAC'S OWN EMAILS SHOW:
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

EVIDENCE A: CONSULTANT ADMISSION THAT FEE REPORTS DON'T SHOW ACTUAL FEES

CITATION: Pi-011, February 23, 2021 email from Sara Davis (Meketa) to 
Veronica Colon (PERAC)

Davis wrote:
"The fee tables shown in our reports are the extent of our fee analysis 
reporting for these clients and are NOT SUPPOSED TO REPRESENT ACTUAL FEES 
PAID OR AN AUDIT."

"We don't include fee estimates for private equity and other closed end fund 
structures in our reporting due to the process being TEDIOUS AND POTENTIALLY 
IMPRECISE due to complex fee structures with carried interest etc."

"We do offer a management and performance fee verification service, but that 
is NOT INCLUDED IN OUR SCOPE OF SERVICES for these clients and additionally 
is QUITE EXPENSIVE due to the time it takes."

"If you have specific questions about a manager, it would be best if you reach 
out to the manager or the client's auditor directly for further clarification."

WHAT THIS SHOWS: Consultant explicitly tells PERAC that standard fee reports 
do not represent actual fees paid. Actual fees for PE investments are not 
calculated because the process is "tedious." Getting actual fees requires 
paying for a separate "quite expensive" service or contacting managers/auditors 
directly.

QUESTION FOR CLARIFICATION: The email shows Veronica Colon asked "Why don't 
all managers have values for fees?" What was PERAC's response to learning that 
fee reports don't show actual fees? Did PERAC require consultants to provide 
actual fee data? If not, why not?


EVIDENCE B: COMPLETE DATA FRAMED AS CAUSING "CONFUSION"

CITATION: Pi-011, February 24, 2021 email from Sara Davis to Veronica Colon

Davis wrote:
"Upon further thought, if we provide both gross and net performance in the 
Trailing Performance Summary for all reports you have mentioned below it would 
then make the 'net/gross column' in the Fee Expense Analysis NO LONGER 
APPLICABLE and may potentially cause MORE CONFUSION THAN CLARITY."

"If you prefer to see both net and gross performance in the Trailing 
Performance Summary, would it be okay if the net/gross column was removed from 
the Fee Expense Analysis due to my reasoning above?"

WHAT THIS SHOWS: Consultant frames providing complete performance data as 
creating "confusion" and asks PERAC to choose between complete performance 
data OR fee expense data.

QUESTION FOR CLARIFICATION: What was PERAC's response to this request? Did 
PERAC accept removing fee expense data to avoid "confusion"? If so, how does 
this protect pension beneficiaries' interest in understanding costs?


EVIDENCE C: PERAC COORDINATED ON FEE REPORTING STANDARDIZATION

SUPPLEMENTAL ANALYSIS: THE $6,250 FEE ESTIMATE PATTERN
================================================================================

CRITICAL DETAIL THAT STRENGTHENS CONTRADICTION 2:
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The $6,250 fee estimate wasn't just provided once - it was REPEATED even after 
the request was narrowed.

THE PATTERN:

CITATION: Pi-004, July 28, 2025 - First fee estimate from William Keefe

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ "Based on the scope of your request, PERAC estimates fees of           │
│ approximately $6,250."                                                  │
│                                                                         │
│ Basis: Claimed need for "extensive search" and "manual reconstruction" │
│ Calculation: Approximately 225 hours of staff time                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

RESPONSE: Requestor narrowed the scope to reduce costs

CITATION: [Subsequent PERAC response - date needed from your records]

PERAC REPEATED THE SAME $6,250 ESTIMATE despite narrowed scope.

WHAT THIS SHOWS:
- Fee estimate did not change when request scope was reduced
- This suggests fee was not based on actual search requirements
- Fee appears designed to DETER requests, not reflect actual costs
- If narrowing scope doesn't reduce fee, the fee is not tied to work required


WHY THIS MATTERS:

Under M.G.L. c. 66, § 10, fees for public records must be based on ACTUAL costs:
- Actual staff time required
- Actual search effort needed
- Reasonable hourly rates

A fee that doesn't change when scope is narrowed is NOT based on actual costs.

Combined with Evidence from Contradiction 2:
- Meketa "spearheaded" uniform reporting (Pi-031)
- PERAC uses ticketing system (Pi-013, 014)
- Records provided were organized, not scattered (Pi-006)
- PERAC compiles complex statewide data internally (Pi-052)

The $6,250 estimate appears to be a "TRANSPARENCY TAX" designed to discourage 
public records requests, not a reflection of actual search costs.

LEGAL IMPLICATIONS:
- Improper denial under M.G.L. c. 66 § 10
- False statements about record availability by public official
- Potential violation of open government laws
- Deterrence of legitimate public oversight

FOR PEOPLE WHO WANT THE BOTTOM LINE:
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Imagine you hired someone to watch over your retirement savings and make sure

- Approve investment plans before they're announced to anyone else

- "Some records might not even exist"

- Everything is organized in a ticketing system

- When forced, they produce organized files quickly
- They even compile complex statewide data for their own internal use

- You ask for records about BlackRock on July 7 at 1am

- Someone logs in 34 times in 9 days, then disappears forever
- No explanation of what they were doing

Meanwhile:
- Fee reports admittedly don't show actual fees
- Getting actual fees costs extra money
- Consultants with worst performance (#100, #94 rankings) keep their jobs
- Important discussions happen on phone calls with no records
- Documents are shared with instructions to "keep under your toga"

THAT'S WHAT THESE CONTRADICTIONS SHOW.

It's not about misunderstanding or different perspectives.

It's about what PERAC says versus what PERAC's own emails prove.

Every contradiction is supported by specific emails with dates, names, and exact 
quotes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Perplexity said:

The draft is very strong on substance and narrative, but it reads more like an investigative brief than a targeted, hard-to-evade public records request. It absolutely surfaces the vendor-email “set up” and the Ford/zzTest patterns, but there are a few ways to make it hit harder, tighten the Conor Ford section, and reduce PERAC’s ability to dodge with “we don’t answer questions” boilerplate.[1][2]

Below are targeted edits, not a full rewrite.

***

## Overall structure and tone

Strengths:
Clear timeline of the $6,250 estimate and contradictions with later productions.[1]
Good use of specific citations (Pi-011, Pi-022, Pi-027, etc.) to anchor claims.
Strong articulation of public interest and fee waiver basis.

Weaknesses:
Long “narrative” sections with many questions invite PERAC to say: “Public Records Law does not require us to answer questions or create explanations.” They have already used that line against you.[1]
Some of the most incriminating issues (Ford 34 logins, test account, vendor emails showing coordination) are embedded in long paragraphs rather than distilled into precise “records sufficient to show…” requests.[2][1]
The legal-risk language (obstruction, conspiracy) is powerful but could cause them to lawyer up and narrow their responses, rather than produce more records.

**Suggestion:** Keep the narrative, but in each section:
- Move the *questions* into “records sufficient to show…” language.
- Reserve explicit “why” questions for a short “Clarifications requested” bullet list at the end of each section, so that even if they refuse to answer questions, the records requests remain clean and enforceable.

***

## Vendor emails and “vague system” setup

You already point out that the vendor communications show:

Meketa “spearheaded” uniform reporting.[1]
Ticketing systems, standardized reporting, and fee report vagueness.[1]
RFP pre-approval, “suggested language,” suspension authority.[2]
If you want to make explicit that these emails show the *set up* of the vague system you are dealing with now, consider a short, explicit bridge paragraph right before SECTION 1:

The vendor emails you produced for 2018–2021 show PERAC and its consultants actively designing standardized “uniform” reporting, vendor ticketing systems, and fee-reporting formats that explicitly avoid representing actual fees paid. These records appear to document the setup of the same vague reporting system and access structure now in use, yet your production stops before 2022. This request seeks the 2022–present continuation of those same systems.[2][1]

This keeps the allegation focused: “continuation of the same systems,” not just “contradictions.”

You could also tighten CONTRADICTION 2 and 3 into a mini-table (more readable, and it visually exposes the pattern):

| PERAC claim | PERAC records show |
| --- | --- |
| “Manual reconstruction” and “extensive search” needed.[1] | Meketa “spearheaded” uniform reporting, ticketing database for vendors, quarterly/annual cycles.[1] |
| Fee transparency and accuracy.[2] | Consultant admits fee tables are “NOT SUPPOSED TO REPRESENT ACTUAL FEES PAID” and “quite expensive” verification is separate.[1] |

***

## Conor Ford / zzTest section: dig deeper but stay FOIA-compliant

Your current 2B is excellent evidence-wise, but it mixes:
- Factual pattern and timeline.
- Records requests.
- Legal argument.

To hit harder and force specific disclosures without giving them an easy “we don’t answer questions” out, adjust as follows.

### 1. Separate “facts” from “records requested”

Under 2B, break into:

**A. Factual access pattern already documented**

Brief 4–5 bullet recap of the pattern (first login ever on July 8, 2025; 34 logins in 9 days; complete cessation after August 19; single zzTest login on September 5; no prior zzTest use in 2020–2024). You already have this in your December 27 request; you can explicitly say “based on PROSPER logs you produced (January 2020–December 2025)”.[1]
This makes clear that *they* created the pattern; you are not speculating.

**B. Records requested (use “records sufficient to show”)**

For example, instead of:

When was this project first discussed? What was the project supposed to achieve?

Use:

All records (emails, memos, tickets, meeting notes, calendar entries, project charters, or work orders) from June 1, 2025 through present that:
Identify or describe the specific project for which BlackRock requested PROSPER access for Brandwein, Xiao, and Ford on July 7, 2025.
Define the project’s scope, objectives, deliverables, and expected completion or termination date.
Document any internal PERAC approval of that project, including risk or access review.[1]
Similarly, for the anonymous zzTest account:

All records sufficient to show for the “FinancialVendor, Test – zzTest PERAC Vendor money manager1” account:
Account creation date and time.
User(s) or entity to whom the account was assigned.
Identity of the PERAC staff who requested, approved, and created the account.
Any policies, tickets, or communications describing its business purpose, allowed use, and any restriction on accessing real data.
Any logs showing what modules, pages, or data that account accessed during its September 5, 2025 session.[1]
For Ford’s 34 sessions:

Detailed PROSPER logs for all Conor Ford sessions in 2025, including for each event:
Timestamp.
Module, page, or file accessed.
Action type (view, download, export, upload, edit, delete, query).
Any record identifiers (e.g., Schedule 7 reports, fee reports, vendor disclosures, or board filings) touched during those sessions.[1]
And for the July 7 awareness of your FOIA:

All PERAC internal and PERAC–BlackRock communications on July 7–8, 2025 that:
Discuss your July 7, 2025 public records request.
Refer to PROSPER access for Brandwein, Xiao, or Ford.
Reference “the request,” “FOIA,” “public records,” or your name in connection with BlackRock access.[2][1]
These formulations still implicitly ask “who” and “why,” but they do it by demanding documents, which they cannot brush off as “questions.”

### 2. Narrow the “legal concern” paragraph

The obstruction section is accurate in concept, but PERAC will likely respond with “we do not provide legal analysis.” You already have a separate, well-developed explanation of their January 7, 2026 response saying BlackRock was not told about your FOIA and that Ford was never physically at PERAC.[1]

You might reduce the “LEGAL CONCERN” block to a single sentence:

Given this unusual temporal pattern, records are necessary to confirm whether vendor access and any test accounts were used solely for routine business or in connection with public records review and data handling decisions.

You can keep the federal/state citations in your blog and in complaints to the Secretary of State or Attorney General; they add less value inside the public records request itself.

***

## Forcing answers vs. creating admissions

The Public Records Law does not require PERAC to *answer* questions, and they have already invoked that repeatedly. To increase the risk of self-incrimination through their responses:[1]

Focus on **yes/no factual gaps** where the *absence* of records is itself telling. For example, in Section 2B, add:
If no records exist that identify any project purpose, deliverables, or closure documentation for Ford’s July–August 2025 PROSPER access, please:
- Confirm in writing that PERAC has no such records.
- Identify the records retention schedule relied on for any destruction of such project documentation.[1]

Do the same for:
Any written policy on test accounts in production systems.
Any policy governing vendor notification when public records requests are received.
Any documented review of access logs for anomalies.
Every time they say “no responsive records,” it strengthens an argument later that the system is either poorly controlled or that they are withholding.

***

## Donor/Ford login: “digging deep enough”?

Your December 27, 2025 refined request already asks extremely detailed questions about Ford, the three credentials, historical access, and zzTest. The Claude draft repeats many of those, but in narrative form. To ensure you “dig deep enough”:[1]

Make sure this new follow-up explicitly cross-references that December 27 request and states:
This follow-up request incorporates by reference my December 27, 2025 refined request, and seeks:
- The same categories of Ford/zzTest PROSPER records for the full 2020–2025 period, and
- Any internal PERAC communications created after December 27, 2025 in response to that refined request.

Add a short “Results of zzTest” clause:
Any test plans, test scripts, bug reports, incident tickets, or summary reports documenting:
The purpose, expected outcome, and actual results of the September 5, 2025 “FinancialVendor, Test – zzTest PERAC Vendor money manager1” session.
The identity of the individual who executed the test and their employer.
Any issues discovered and remediation actions taken.[1]
This hits directly the “Who performed the zzTest and what were the results?” question in a records-focused way.

***

## $6,250 fee and forcing them to reconcile

You already have their Jan 7, 2026 letter with detailed hour estimates and their repeated use of 6,250/6,575. The draft questions here are on point; to make it harder to dodge:[1]

Explicitly ask for:
All internal timekeeping, billing, or task-tracking records used to calculate:
- The 30 hours attributed to IT for PROSPER logs.
- The 140 hours attributed to compliance/investment staff.
- The 80 hours attributed to legal review.[1]

And:
All drafts, internal emails, or notes discussing how to respond to my fee-waiver arguments and whether to adjust the fee estimate for my narrowed scope.[1]

Again, the idea is to tie their 6,250 math back to actual time records; if those don’t exist, the gap is incriminating in itself.

***

## Does the email “force” incriminating answers?

A public records request cannot compel them to *admit* wrongdoing, but it can:

Force them to:
Admit records exist and produce them, or
Admit records don’t exist despite legal/compliance expectations, or
Assert exemptions that look strained given the subject matter.
Your draft already moves in this direction. With the revisions above:

You make it harder for them to hide behind “we don’t answer questions.”
You sharpen the focus on:
The design and continuation of the vague vendor-reporting system.
The unexplained Ford/zzTest access pattern.
The mismatch between organized systems and the 6,250 narrative.[2][1]
That combination maximizes the chance that whatever they say (or fail to say) can be used later in appeals or external complaints.

SECTION 3: THE CD WORKAROUND - INTENTIONAL RECORD-KEEPING BARRIER
================================================================================

CITATION: Pi-027 (May-December 2021) - "Boston R.B. CD AUG - OCT (maybe NOV

This email thread discusses using physical CDs (compact discs) to provide data

ANALYSIS:

The use of physical CDs in 2021 - when cloud-based systems, SFTP, and email 
transfer are standard - is not a matter of technical limitation. It is an 
intentional barrier to audit, searchability, and transparency.

A CD in 2021 is not a storage choice; it is a denial strategy.

Modern audit tools, database queries, and AI analysis systems cannot process 
data locked on physical media. Physical CDs ensure that:
- Data cannot be searched electronically
- Analysis tools cannot process the information
- Public records requests are more difficult to fulfill
- Historical data becomes effectively inaccessible

Both vendors and PERAC know this. The intent matters.

   • Whether this practice is intended to limit searchability or public access
   • How physical media delivery aligns with modern records management standards

3. All records sufficient to show instances where retirement systems or vendors:
   • Requested electronic data but received physical media instead

   • Experienced delays or difficulties due to physical media delivery

Perplexity said:
This draft is a clear improvement over the prior one in a few key ways, but there are also places where it gets a bit weaker or gives PERAC easy “outs.”[1][2]

## Where this draft is stronger

**Much tighter FOIA framing:**  
Heavy use of “records sufficient to show…” language fixes the problem of them replying “we don’t answer questions” while still targeting the same facts (Ford, zzTest, fee estimate, etc.).[1]
The sections on PROSPER logs, Ford, zzTest, fee estimate, and internal communications are now structured in a way that is easier for the Supervisor of Records to enforce.

**Better linkage between 2018–2021 emails and today’s “vague system”:**  
You explicitly state that Pi-031 (uniform reporting), ticketing (Pi-013, Pi-014), and fee-report design choices document the setup of the current system and that you are asking for the 2022–present continuation of those same systems.[1]
The small comparison table on “PERAC stated vs PERAC’s own records show” is sharp and readable.

**Conor Ford/zzTest section now “digs deep enough”:**  
You’ve successfully converted “who/why” questions into demands for project charters, approvals, logs, test plans, and retention-schedule citations.[1]
Adding the “if no records exist, confirm in writing and identify retention schedule” clause is exactly what you want for later appeals.

**Fee estimate and internal strategy:**  
Section 7 on internal communications/timekeeping directly targets the 30/140/80 hour breakdown in Pi-007 and forces them either to produce backing records or admit they don’t exist.[1]

Overall, this version “hits harder” on the Ford / zzTest / fee-estimate areas **without** overplaying accusations in the body of the request.

## Where it gets weaker or gives PERAC openings

**YES/NO question about Ford accessing responsive records**

The explicit “Did Conor Ford… access or view records responsive to my July 7 request?” is the kind of direct question they can refuse to answer as “not required under Public Records Law.”[1]
That doesn’t help you much because the real leverage is in the logs and internal communications, not their yes/no narrative.
**Fix:** Drop the standalone YES/NO block and instead add to item 3 in 2B:

Please also identify, for each Ford session, whether any document later produced in response to my July 7, 2025 request was accessed or modified during that session.

That forces the same admission through records rather than an answer to a question.

**CD section rhetoric (“denial strategy”)**

The analysis sentence “A CD in 2021 is not a storage choice; it is a denial strategy” is rhetorically powerful but exposes you to the same “we don’t answer accusations/opinions” line.[1]
The records you actually want (communications about physical media, policy, correlation with sensitive data) are already strong; you don’t need to state intent so bluntly inside the request.
**Fix:** Keep the critique but soften intent:

In 2021, choosing physical CDs instead of standard electronic transfer has the practical effect of limiting searchability and making public records production materially more burdensome.

You can reserve the “denial strategy” language for your blog and complaints.

**Some over-broad “all communications” that will trigger big fee estimates**

Section 1 (vendor communications 2022–present for “any investment consultant, investment manager, or financial services vendor”) is extremely broad and could easily generate another “tens of thousands of emails” estimate like the 27,000-email letter.[1]
Section 7.1 (“all internal communications regarding public records requests received in July 2025”) plus Section 1 plus Section 5 plus Section 6 on performance might collectively be used to justify a large fee again.
**Fix options (you can pick one):**
Narrow Section 1 to:
Named vendor groups (BlackRock, Meketa, Hamilton Lane) and PRIM; or
Communications containing specific keywords (e.g., “Schedule 7,” “fee report,” “uniformity,” “the plan”) rather than *all* vendor communications.
Or expressly offer to prioritize:
“If the full scope is deemed burdensome, please first produce: (i) 2022–present BlackRock/Meketa/Hamilton Lane communications; (ii) PRIM communications re vendor evaluations; (iii) any records referencing ‘uniformity’ or ‘the plan’.”

**A few places still mix argument and request in ways they can sidestep**

Section 3’s “Both vendors and PERAC know this. The intent matters.” and Section 4’s a/b/c motives for “confusion” are correct analytically but give them a chance to respond with generalities instead of focusing on records.[1]
The “WHY COMPLETE TRANSPARENCY IS NECESSARY” block is strong as justification, but any “are deliberately concealed” phrasing is again not enforceable under c.66.
**Fix:** You can keep this policy/advocacy material, but if you want to be maximally hard to dodge, keep argument short and let the specific records requests do the work.

## Does it still highlight the setup of the current vague system?

Yes, better than before:

It explicitly ties:
2018–2021 vendor emails (uniform reporting, ticketing, “NOT SUPPOSED TO REPRESENT ACTUAL FEES PAID”) to
2022–present records you’re requesting as the continuation of those systems.[2][1]
Section 4 on fee reporting plus Section 5 on RFP “expectations/the plan” together describe the vague system’s architecture: reporting design, fee omission, and PERAC’s informal role.
If you want to press this point even more cleanly, you could add a one-sentence bridge at the end of the “RECONCILIATION OF ADMINISTRATIVE CONTRADICTIONS” section:

The 2022–present records requested below are necessary to determine whether the same uniform, vague reporting and coordination practices documented in 2018–2021 were extended, expanded, or modified after those emails.[2][1]

## Net assessment

**Improved over the last draft:**  
Yes. It is more surgical, more FOIA-compliant, and more likely to survive a “we don’t answer questions” response while still pressing the Ford/zzTest and fee contradictions.[2][1]

**New weaknesses:**  
The main soft spots are (a) the explicit yes/no Ford question, (b) the “denial strategy” rhetoric around CDs, and (c) breadth of some “all communications” requests that may invite another large fee estimate.

Current approach (what I wrote):

Result: Could be 1,000+ emails including scheduling, spam, irrelevant stuff
Perplexity's approach:

Perplexity said: 
This version is much closer to your actual goal: it reframes their estimate using their own records, narrows the live records request into four small sets, and builds a path to either cooperation or escalation. Overall, it “hits” well strategically, but it is still long, and the Option C / “regulatory capture” language could make them defensive rather than responsive.

Here’s a focused read on strengths and refinements.

## Strong elements

**Directly addresses the $6,250 estimate with concrete contradictions**  
Tying their “manual reconstruction from scattered sources” claim to Pi‑031 (uniformity), Pi‑052 (systematic RFP tracking), Pi‑013/014 (ticketing), and Pi‑027 (CDs) is exactly the right move; it undercuts the premise of their cost estimate using their own documents.[1]

**Separates “internal investigation” from “revised records request”**  
Asking them to look at contradictions as an internal integrity issue *before* you sink money into records is smart and hard to dismiss as frivolous.[1]

**Request Sets A–D are finally small and specific**  
Each set asks for a handful of clearly existing items (one work order, one log export, one sample standard/verification pair, one policy, one database, etc.) and even provides conservative time/cost estimates. That aligns with their own invitation to narrow by specific items.[1]

**Fee waiver section is solid**  
You tick the classic boxes: public interest, non‑commercial purpose, personal financial hardship, and minimal burden, all grounded in the scale of PERAC’s mandate and your disability income.[1]

## What to consider toning down or trimming

If the priority is getting the records and lowering the fee, not persuading them of “regulatory capture” in this email, a few adjustments will help.

### 1. Tone and threat structure (Options A–C)

PART 9’s “Option C” (public scandal, media, regulatory capture) and the repeated “I will escalate” framing may push this into “adversarial” territory in their minds, which can slow or harden responses even if legally they still owe the records.
You can keep the *substance* (that you will complain to the Supervisor of Records, Auditor, etc.) but make it more procedural and less dramatic.
Suggestion:

Reframe “Option C” as:

“If PERAC declines to investigate and does not provide the requested records, I will pursue available remedies, including appeals to the Supervisor of Records and, if appropriate, referrals to oversight entities and media.”

This keeps the leverage but drops some of the prosecutorial language.

### 2. Length and repetition

The email is very long; staff skimming may only see the “pressure” parts and miss how narrow your actual request sets are.
You repeat the contradictions in Part 1, then again in Part 3 as numbered investigation areas. Keeping both is fine, but consider tightening Part 3 to just a few lines per topic, since Part 6 (Request Sets A–D) already operationalizes the same issues.
You might:

Keep the clear CLAIM/PROVE/CONTRADICTION blocks in Part 1 (they’re good).
In Part 3, compress each issue to a single bullet and point straight to the relevant Request Set, e.g.:

“Fee reporting discrepancy (Pi‑011, Pi‑031) – see Request Set B.”

This reinforces that you’ve translated the contradictions into small, concrete records requests.

### 3. “Systematic regulatory capture” framing

You’ve removed that phrase from the subject line, which is good. There are still several uses of “regulatory capture” and “cover‑up” language later.
For an RAO and counsel, that language mostly signals “this will become litigation/media” and encourages them to be defensive.
If your first goal is to get Request Sets A–D at low or waived cost, consider:

Keep your *logic* (A/B/C possibilities, documented contradictions).
Swap “regulatory capture” with more neutral phrasing, e.g. “serious governance and oversight concerns.”
You can always use the stronger phrase in public writing and complaints.

### 4. Clarify that Request Sets A–D replace, not add to, the old request

To avoid them piggybacking the old 6,250 estimate onto this, add one line near PART 6:

“This revised request supersedes and narrows my prior December 2025 requests for the purposes of fee estimation; please calculate a fresh estimate based solely on Request Sets A–D.”[1]

That signals clearly that your operative ask is the four small sets, not the earlier broad scopes.

## Micro‑edits that strengthen your position

In Request Set A, explicitly tie the Ford logs to the constrained dates and identities you already documented from PROSPER logs: Conor Ford and the BlackRock accounts in July–August 2025, not “all BlackRock logs forever.”[1]

In Request Set C, for the list of RFPs PERAC reviewed, you can narrow initial scope to the ones already in Pi files (Quincy, Concord, Natick, MWRA) plus “any others for which PERAC retains a centralized log of RFP reviews.” That keeps it looking like a bounded retrieval from an index, not an open‑ended historical study.[1]

For Request Set D, instead of “any similar analysis for 2019–2024,” you might say:

“any existing analyses similar to ‘2018 MA Consultant RFPs’ (i.e., compiled RFP outcome summaries for later years), to the extent they are already maintained.”

That avoids implying they must create new cross‑year analysis.

## Bottom line

This approach is substantially better aligned with:

your financial constraints,
the legal framework around “narrow, specific” requests, and
the record you are trying to build showing contradictions between PERAC’s statements and its own files.[1]
With modest tone‑downs (particularly in Parts 8–10) and a clearer statement that Request Sets A–D supersede the prior broad request for fee purposes, this is a strong, credible next move that forces a much lower estimate and makes any refusal look unreasonable if you later appeal or go public.[1]
